research_question: In adults with coronary heart disease, heart failure, or atrial fibrillation, what is the effect of a psychological intervention—delivered alone, alongside cardiac rehabilitation, or alongside pharmacotherapy—compared with no psychological intervention on validated depression symptom scores at the longest available follow-up from 6 through 12 months after randomisation?
treatment_label: Psychological intervention, delivered alone or as an adjunct to cardiac rehabilitation or pharmacotherapy
control_label: No psychological intervention (e.g., usual care, wait-list, attention control, cardiac rehabilitation alone, pharmacotherapy alone, or an otherwise matched non-psychological comparator)
outcome_description: Depression symptoms measured with any validated depression instrument (including BDI, BDI-II, BDI-FS, CDS, HADS-D, HAM-D, PHQ-9, and ZDS) at an eligible follow-up of 6 to 12 months after randomisation. Treat all instruments as measures of one common depression construct and pool them as standardized mean differences. For each eligible intervention-control comparison, select exactly one depression endpoint: the longest available follow-up within the inclusive 6-to-12-month window. Evaluate depression only; do not extract, classify, or pool anxiety, health-related quality of life, self-efficacy, mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events, or any other outcome.
positive_direction: A positive effect means fewer depression symptoms in the psychological-intervention group than in the no-psychological-intervention group after orienting all scales so that improvement favors the intervention.
search_queries: coronary heart disease psychological intervention depression randomized trial
heart failure psychotherapy depression controlled trial
atrial fibrillation psychological treatment depression experiment
inclusion_criteria: Original empirical studies of adults with coronary heart disease, heart failure, or atrial fibrillation that compare a psychological intervention with a condition receiving no psychological intervention; psychological treatment may be delivered alone or added to cardiac rehabilitation or pharmacotherapy when the comparison isolates the psychological component.
Randomised studies reporting depression symptoms using any validated depression measure at one or more follow-ups within 6 to 12 months after randomisation.

Studies providing, or allowing derivation of, quantitative depression data for an intervention-control comparison; include any setting, delivery format, psychological approach, publication status, and language.
exclusion_criteria: Not an original empirical study; exclude systematic reviews, meta-analyses, editorials, opinion pieces, protocols without results, and theoretical papers.

No comparison between a psychological-intervention condition and a control condition receiving no psychological intervention, or co-interventions are not sufficiently matched to isolate the psychological component.

No quantitative depression outcome data that can produce an effect size, such as means and standard deviations, t/F statistics, proportions, or odds ratios, and the required data cannot be obtained or derived.

Completely unrelated to psychological intervention, depression, or adults with coronary heart disease, heart failure, or atrial fibrillation; also exclude reports with no validated depression endpoint in the 6-to-12-month post-randomisation window.
moderators_to_extract: cardiac diagnosis (coronary heart disease, heart failure, or atrial fibrillation)
psychological intervention type or therapeutic orientation
delivery context (stand-alone, with cardiac rehabilitation, or with pharmacotherapy)
delivery format and provider (individual, group, digital/telephone, or mixed)
eligible follow-up time selected in months
effect_size_note: Pool standardized mean differences across validated depression instruments, with scale direction harmonized so positive values indicate lower depression in the intervention group. Prefer Hedges-corrected SMDs in estimation if supported by the analysis workflow. Use exactly one endpoint per eligible intervention-control comparison: the longest available assessment within 6 to 12 months after randomisation (inclusive). Do not split results by depression instrument or by follow-up time. For multi-arm studies, avoid double-counting shared controls by combining eligible intervention arms when clinically appropriate or otherwise accounting for the dependency. Use an appropriate random-effects model, report 95% confidence intervals and heterogeneity, assess risk of bias at the outcome level, and document screening and exclusions in a PRISMA 2020 flow diagram.
